title: The Pythagorean Theorem
short: In a right triangle, a² + b² = c², shown by rearranging squares.
trouble: Students use a leg as c, or add the sides before squaring.

blocks.html: In a right triangle, the two sides that form the right angle are the legs, and the side across from the right angle is the hypotenuse, always the longest side. Their lengths are tied together by a rule that uses squares and square roots.

Take four copies of a right triangle with legs $a$ and $b$ and hypotenuse $c$, and place them inside a big square with sides $a + b$. Arranged one way, they leave a tilted square of area $c^{2}$ uncovered in the middle. Slide them into two rectangles instead, and the uncovered part becomes two squares, of areas $a^{2}$ and $b^{2}$. The big square and the four triangles never changed, so the uncovered areas must be equal: $a^{2} + b^{2} = c^{2}$.

blocks.name: pythagoras
blocks.cap: Press “Slide the triangles” to watch the $c^{2}$ square become $a^{2}$ plus $b^{2}$.

blocks.html: Pythagorean theorem: in a right triangle with legs $a$ and $b$ and hypotenuse $c$, $$a^{2} + b^{2} = c^{2}$$

blocks.cap: The squares on the legs, $9 + 16$, cover exactly as much as the square on the hypotenuse, $25$. Change the legs and count again.

blocks.title: Find the hypotenuse
blocks.q: A right triangle has legs 6 and 8. Find the hypotenuse.

blocks.title: Find a leg
blocks.q: A right triangle has hypotenuse 13 and one leg 5. Find the other leg.

blocks.title: An irrational length
blocks.q: A right triangle has legs 2 and 3. Find the hypotenuse.
steps: 13 is not a perfect square, so $c = \sqrt{13}$, about 3.6.

blocks.html: Two slips. Using a leg as $c$: $c$ is always the side across from the right angle, the longest side, so when you know the hypotenuse, you subtract to find a leg. And adding before squaring: for legs 6 and 8, $(6 + 8)^{2} = 196$ is not $6^{2} + 8^{2} = 100$. Square each leg first.
